q: What are the five parts of a prompt written as a working brief?
options: Outcome, audience and situation, material, limits, format
explain: Write a prompt the way you'd brief a new colleague: outcome, audience and situation, material to use, limits to respect, form of a useful result.

q: Uploading a LOOP product sheet to an assistant…
options: Gives the model working information for this task only
Has no effect on the output
explain: Context supplies working information; model training is a separate process. Students often confuse the two.

q: An AI draft says “LOOP keeps drinks cold for 24 hours”, but the product sheet says nothing about insulation. What should the assistant do?
options: Keep the claim — it's typical for steel bottles
Remove the bottle size too, to be safe
Flag it as unsupported, ask for test data, and use only known facts
Replace it with “keeps drinks cold all day”
explain: It should flag the claim, ask for test data and propose wording limited to known facts (750 ml, steel) — not quietly keep it.

q: Which is an example of predictive (not generative) AI?
options: A first draft of an ad
explain: Predictive estimates an outcome; generative creates an output. Real workflows often mix both.

q: Search spent €600 and drove 60 purchases. What is the CPA?
explain: CPA = spend ÷ purchases = €600 ÷ 60 = €10.00.

q: In the LOOP pilot, why does ROAS rank channels exactly as CPA does?
options: Because spend was equal per channel
Because every purchase is exactly one €29 bottle
Because retargeting has the most impressions
explain: With constant order value, revenue is just purchases × €29, so revenue doesn't change the channel story.

q: Why might retargeting's strong ROAS (4.35) be misleading?
options: It reaches mostly people already interested, so attribution flatters it
Its data is real while the rest is synthetic
explain: Retargeting reaches people already interested and depends on prospecting to fill its audience.

q: Noy & Zhang (Science, 2023) found that with ChatGPT on writing tasks…
explain: 453 professionals; time fell about 40% and graded quality rose about 18%. Limits: specific tasks, an older model, graders didn't fact-check.

q: Why can't LOOP claim to be “the most sustainable bottle in Europe”?
options: EU Directive 2024/825 (EmpCo) bars generic environmental claims without recognised evidence
Because LOOP only sells in Barcelona
explain: Since 27 September 2026, EmpCo bars generic environmental claims unless recognised excellent environmental performance can be shown.

q: A weekly AI campaign report needs four things. Which is NOT one of them?
explain: The four: schedule and data source, comparison period, a threshold (e.g. CPA moves >20%), and a named reviewer.

q: Which analytics level answers “What should we do?”
explain: Descriptive: what happened. Predictive: what will happen. Prescriptive: the system recommends the action.

q: In the Euromon PLV audit, what was the AI's only source?
options: The professor's own deleted Reddit post from July 2024
explain: It repeated what it had read rather than diagnosing anything — the site was no longer on Wix.

q: Given a two-week Search Console export instead of screenshots, what did the AI conclude?
options: A Google anti-spam update hit the whole site
3 pages account for 97% of the loss; the rest is stable
explain: Same AI, same question, opposite answer depending on input. Clicks actually went from 7 to 8.

q: What does GEO stand for?
explain: Publishing content so generative engines (like ChatGPT) surface your brand — e.g. Euromon PLV listed first by Oct 2026.

q: Higgsfield's banners claimed 55% and 62% off. What did Plus actually get?
explain: Inflated percentages, countdown timers, “personal” framing and exit-intent offers were the tactics on show.

q: Roughly what share of Netflix viewing comes from recommendations (Gomez-Uribe & Hunt, 2015)?
explain: About 80% — an example of technology as a strategic asset rather than a support function.

q: Why was Amazon's CV-scoring AI scrapped in 2017?
options: Amazon couldn't guarantee it wouldn't discriminate in other ways
explain: Trained on mostly male CVs, it marked down CVs containing “women's”.

q: Which guardrail responds to the black-box problem?
explain: Bias → audits and diverse data. Privacy → privacy by design. Transparency → a human in the loop.

q: How is Web Analytics assessed?
explain: Coursework is graded by TFM tutors, partly on fit with your TFM case and strategy.

q: In the AI agent trading desks, what is the sceptic agent for?
options: Explaining why the other agents might be wrong
Approving every trade instead of a human
explain: Without it, the agents just agree with each other.

q: What are the four pillars of a CRM?
explain: Technology + AI is the enabler that centralises, automates and anticipates — not the goal.

q: In the CRM methodology, what starts a process?
explain: Every process has four elements: target, trigger, content, channel. The trigger is the action or event that starts it.

q: “You're running out of dog food: shall we send some?” is an example of which experience approach?
explain: Predictive: AI anticipates needs not yet expressed. Proactive gets ahead of a known problem.

q: Which AI use fits the Retention stage of the lifecycle?
explain: Acquisition: lead scoring · Conversion: conversational agents · Growth: next best offer · Retention: churn prediction · Reactivation: smart campaigns.

q: Which system answers “Who is this person across all our systems?”
explain: A CDP unifies data from several systems into a single profile.

q: Which AI layer belongs to HubSpot?
explain: Salesforce → Agentforce · HubSpot → Breeze · Dynamics 365 → Copilot · Zoho → Zia.

q: Under the EU AI Act, what applies from August 2026?
options: Transparency: tell people they're talking to an AI and label generated content
High-risk systems such as credit scoring
explain: Feb 2025: AI literacy and prohibited practices · Aug 2026: transparency · Dec 2027: high-risk (postponed by the Digital Omnibus).

q: GDPR Article 22 gives people the right…
options: Not to be subject to solely automated decisions
explain: Relevant whenever a CRM automates decisions about customers.

q: In the abandoned-cart example, what's the content rule the first time?
options: Products and size in stock, no discount
explain: AI adds value by predicting who'll buy without an incentive, so no margin is given away.

q: A DMP mainly relies on…
options: First-party data in a unified hub
Anonymous third-party data, usually expiring after ~90 days
explain: DMPs build audience segments for ads; the phase-out of third-party cookies is a challenge for them.

q: Which is listed as a common pitfall with AI-powered CDPs?
options: Enforcing consent at the profile layer
explain: Training models on fragmented data leads to compounding errors. Other pitfalls: treating a prediction as a strategy, starting too big.

q: Which is NOT one of the three ethics questions before you automate?
options: Is it cheaper than a person?
explain: Trust is a CRM's most valuable asset.

q: Which of these is NOT one of the 7Ds of digital marketing?
explain: The 7Ds: goals, audiences, devices, platforms, media, data and technology.

q: In Smart Insights’ RACE system, what happens in the “Action” stage?
options: Build a tactical roadmap, often as agile 90-day plans
explain: Opportunity = situation review · Strategy = choose initiatives · Action = execution roadmap.

q: BCG’s rule “Place big bets” means…
options: Spread budget across as many pilots as possible
Focus on two or three high-value use cases, short-term wins first
explain: The five rules: assess impact, set high ambitions, place big bets, build new muscles, manage transformation actively.

q: In a SWOT, “outdated tech” belongs in…
explain: Weaknesses are internal factors that detract from your competitive edge.

q: According to the reading, where does the real value of a SWOT lie?
options: Prioritising the top 3–5 items per category and turning them into actions
explain: Step 6: prioritise and take action.

q: HelloFresh meal kits vs a food delivery app is an example of which competitor type?
explain: Indirect: different offering, same core customer need.

q: How does PEST differ from SWOT?
options: PEST looks only at the external macro-environment
PEST is used only for individuals
explain: PEST is often the main input for SWOT’s Opportunities and Threats.

q: Which is NOT one of the 3 core pillars of SEO in the reading?
explain: The three pillars: indexation, keyword/prompt research, intent-driven content.

q: “Nike login” is which type of search intent?
explain: Navigational: the user wants to find a specific site.

q: Roughly what share of all web searches are long-tail variations?
explain: Head terms ≈10–15%, mid-length ≈15–20%, long-tail ≈70%.

q: Why do long-tail keywords usually give a better ROAS in paid search?
options: Less bidding competition means a lower CPC
explain: Lower CPC plus visitors closer to purchase.

q: Which tool is described as the “source of truth” for search volume and CPC, straight from Google Ads?
explain: Search Console audits your own site’s queries; Keyword Planner gives raw volume, seasonality and CPC.

q: Which metric is described as the ultimate baseline UX metric?
explain: TSR: the % of users who complete a defined task, e.g. a checkout.

q: A System Usability Scale score of 82 is…
explain: Above 68 is average; above 80 is world class.

q: Why is NPS called a lagging indicator of UX quality compared to CES?
options: It measures long-term loyalty rather than the ease of a specific interaction
It is collected less often by law
explain: CES asks how easy today’s interaction was; NPS measures likelihood to recommend over time.

q: Which is an attitudinal (user feedback) metric rather than a behavioural one?
explain: Behavioural metrics are tracked automatically; attitudinal ones come from user feedback.

q: In the CUPID score, what does the “P” stand for?
explain: Convenience, Understanding, Personalisation, Intimacy, Data.

q: In Deliverable 1, each buyer persona must be classified as…
explain: The brief asks to distinguish whether a persona is a brand lover, loyal or occasional customer.

q: How many followers did the boutique account @jackobbuczynskigarage have on 28 Oct 2026?
explain: 343 is the baseline; the proposed Oct 2027 target is 3,000. 96.9k is the main account.

q: What do the research reports identify as the main reason Barcelona Reels lost reach?
options: Distribution: Polish captions reaching people who can’t visit
explain: People who saw the September Reels engaged well (≈3.6% per view); the content reached the wrong country.

q: How many hours a week is the Gràcia boutique open, compared with nearby vintage shops?
Which hashtags put the boutique in the “cheapest, most crowded category”?
explain: The plan repositions it from vintage/thrift to an upcycling atelier and experience.

q: SEO improves a website's visibility in which results?
explain: SEO is about organic (unpaid) results; ads and shopping are paid search.

q: What are the three steps from publishing a page to ranking?
explain: Bots crawl (discover) the page, store it in the index, then rank it for queries.

q: "iPhone X store Barcelona" is which type of search intent?
explain: A place in the query signals local intent. "Buy iPhone X" is transactional, "iPhone X features" informational.

q: "iPhone X" on its own is classed as…
explain: With no modifier you can't tell what the user wants, so it's ambiguous.

q: Which tool shows search engine market share by country?
explain: Statcounter shows market share by country and period: the starting point for choosing engines per market.

q: The keyword principle from class is…
options: As many keywords as possible per page
explain: Each target keyword (search intent) gets its own relevant page.

q: Which on-site element is noted as no longer a ranking factor?
explain: The meta description still affects clicks (CTR) but not rankings.

q: In keyword selection you look for…
options: The best balance of ranking difficulty and potential traffic
The highest volume regardless of difficulty
The lowest difficulty regardless of volume
explain: High volume with impossible difficulty brings nothing; easy terms with no volume bring nothing either.

q: How do you see a page the way Google sees it (its source code)?
explain: Ctrl + U opens view-source: Google reads the code, not the design.

q: Which is NOT a reason a page's ranking fluctuates?
options: The page reached position 1, so it's fixed
Changes to your content or links
explain: Rankings are never permanent: your changes, competitors' changes and algorithm updates all move them.

q: What does INP measure in Core Web Vitals?
explain: LCP = loading, INP = interactivity, CLS = visual stability.

q: CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) measures…
explain: CLS tracks how much the layout jumps around while loading.

q: The "air fryer" SERP is mostly informational. Where should you target that keyword?
explain: Match the search intent (RankBrain): informational queries rank blog content, not product pages.

q: According to Search Engine Journal, the top three ranking factors are…
options: Keywords in meta tags, HTTPS, domain age
explain: New factors keep arriving, but quality content (which earns links) stays the base.

q: Google Panda (2011) mainly targeted…
options: Low-quality and duplicate content, spam, malware
explain: Panda cleaned the SERPs of thin, duplicate and spammy content. Links were Penguin's job.

q: Google Penguin targets…
explain: Penguin hits reciprocal-link overuse, keyword-rich anchors, keyword stuffing and bought links.

q: Roughly what share of a natural link profile uses brand or non-descriptive anchor text?
explain: About 70% brand/non-descriptive anchors; the rest exact or phrase match.

q: BERT helps Google to…
options: Understand the intent and context of a query
explain: BERT is NLP: individual words matter less, search intent more.

q: What does E-E-A-T stand for?
explain: Google's quality raters guidelines; especially important for YMYL content.

q: YMYL content is…
options: Content that can affect health, money, legal or safety decisions
explain: Your Money or Your Life: health, financial, legal, safety and life-affecting content, held to higher standards.

q: The Mobile-First Index means Google…
options: Indexes and ranks the mobile version of a site
explain: Launched Oct 2017, fully rolled out 2021. Different content on mobile vs desktop can hurt rankings.

q: Where must robots.txt be placed?
options: In the root of the domain
explain: Bots look for /robots.txt at the domain root.

q: Which method can de-index a page that is already in Google's index?
explain: noindex keeps pages out of the index and removes indexed ones.

q: You move your site to a new domain. How do you transfer rankings and link equity?
explain: A 301 says "moved permanently" and passes authority to the new URL; it's the only way to transfer it all.

q: A canonical URL is…
options: The "master" version of duplicate or near-duplicate pages
The shortest URL on the site
explain: Google indexes and shows the canonical version of a set of similar pages.

q: Which site architecture is recommended for SEO?
explain: The more clicks (crawl depth) to reach a page, the less relevant it seems. Fewer clicks is better.

q: Which structured-data format does Google recommend?
explain: Schema markup can be JSON-LD, Microdata or RDFa; Google recommends JSON-LD.

q: The "halo effect" in SEO means…
options: Ranking for many long-tail keywords with one root makes the short-head keyword easier
Brand searches lift all pages equally
explain: Long-tail wins with the same root build relevance for the competitive head term and synonyms.

q: Good practice for links per page is…
explain: Fewer clicks, under 100 links per page, logical semantic links.

q: Why doesn't a new sitemap guarantee quick crawling?
options: Google must know about it: submit it in Search Console
It must be printed in the footer
explain: Submit the sitemap URL in GSC so Google crawls the site more often.

q: Backlinks are part of…
explain: Links from other sites are off-page factors.

q: Which is worth more?
explain: Link variety: diversity of linking domains matters.

q: Which link placement is the most valuable?
options: In the main content, near the start
explain: <main> content > sidebar > footer.

q: Domain Authority (DA) is…
options: A Moz score (1–100) predicting ranking potential, not used by Google
explain: Moz created DA around 2010. Useful to compare sites; Google doesn't use it.

q: A Private Blog Network (B → A, A → C, C → B) is…
options: A link scheme that violates Google's spam policy
explain: Link schemes are black-hat SEO and harm rankings.

q: The skyscraper technique means…
options: Improving outdated popular content and telling those who linked to it
Building the tallest page on the site
explain: Make the better version, then ask the existing linkers to point to yours.

q: Asking a site that mentions your brand to add a link is called…
explain: Turn brand mentions without a link into backlinks.

q: Recommended alt text for a Google Images keyword is…
options: A descriptive phrase of up to 8 words with the keyword
explain: Include the keyword, max ~8 words; "photo" or "image" can help.

q: Target file size for images is…
explain: Light images, .webp for better compression.

q: How far back does the Search Console Performance report go?
explain: Position, impressions, CTR and clicks for up to 16 months.

q: Which is NOT a Search Console verification method?
explain: Methods: HTML file, HTML meta tag, DNS record, Google Analytics, Google Tag Manager.

q: Which GSC report shows why URLs are excluded from the index?
explain: Pages shows indexed vs excluded URLs with reasons such as robots.txt or noindex.

q: Screaming Frog is…
options: An SEO spider that crawls sites and collects titles, headers and meta data
A keyword volume tool from Google
explain: Useful for auditing your own and competitors' sites.

q: In the Café Metro "Pay with a Kiss" case, the coffee cost…
options: A kiss and a Facebook share
explain: 1,016 kisses in 2 months, 140 media outlets, $2.4M AUD earned media value.

q: A Veblen good is one where…
options: Demand rises as the price rises
Demand falls as the price rises
explain: Status-driven demand, shown with the ugly-sneakers example.
